{{Short description|Square matrix whose off-diagonal entries are nonpositive}}
{{For|the chemistry related meaning of this term|Z-matrix (chemistry)}}

In [[mathematics]], the class of ''Z''-matrices are those [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] whose off-diagonal entries are less than or equal to zero; that is, the matrices of the form:

:<math>Z=(z_{ij});\quad z_{ij}\leq 0, \quad i\neq j.</math>

This definition coincides precisely with that of a '''negated''' [[Metzler matrix]] or [[quasipositive matrix]], thus the term ''quasinegative'' matrix appears from time to time in the literature, though this is rare and usually only in contexts where references to quasipositive matrices are made.

The [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of a '''competitive''' dynamical system is a ''Z''-matrix by definition. Likewise, if the Jacobian of a '''cooperative''' dynamical system is ''J'', then (&minus;''J'') is a ''Z''-matrix.

Related classes are [[L-matrix|''L''-matrices]], [[M-matrix|''M''-matrices]], [[P-matrix|''P''-matrices]], [[Hurwitz-stable matrix|''Hurwitz'' matrices]] and [[Metzler matrix|''Metzler'' matrices]].  ''L''-matrices have the additional property that all diagonal entries are greater than zero.  M-matrices have several equivalent definitions, one of which is as follows: a ''Z''-matrix is an ''M''-matrix if it is [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|nonsingular]] and its inverse is nonnegative.  All matrices that are both ''Z''-matrices and ''P''-matrices are nonsingular ''M''-matrices.

In the context of [[quantum complexity theory]], these are referred to as ''stoquastic operators''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Bravyi|first1 = Sergey|last2 = DiVincenzo|first2 = David P.|last3 = Oliveira|first3 = Roberto I.|last4 = Terhal|first4 = Barbara M. |title=The complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonian problems |journal=Quantum Information & Computation |volume=8 |issue=5 |pages=361–385 |date=2008 | doi=10.26421/QIC8.5-1 |orig-date=2006 |arxiv=quant-ph/0606140}}</ref>

==Example==

As per the definition, all elements not on the main diagonal are less than or equal to zero.

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
  \begin{pmatrix}
     1 & -2 &  0 \\
     0 &  5 & -1 \\
    -1 & -3 & -4 \\
  \end{pmatrix}
\end{align}</math>
